name: Silvaner

lines.s10: Silvaner is Franken's dry white, bottled in a round flask: pear, green apple and fresh hay, gentle and made for the table.
lines.s20: Silvaner is a dry German white, at home in Franken and Rheinhessen. It is gentle and savoury, with pear, green apple and a scent of fresh hay, and it is the wine Germans pour with white asparagus.
lines.s45: Silvaner is what Germany pours when the white asparagus arrives. It makes a dry white, at home in Franken, around Würzburg, and in Rheinhessen. It tastes of pear, green apple and honeydew melon, with a scent of fresh hay and a savoury note like damp earth. The acidity is gentle and the body medium, so nothing shouts. Growers make it in steel or big old casks, with no new oak. Besides asparagus, pour it with river fish, shellfish or a plate of ham. In Franken it comes in the Bocksbeutel, a flat, round flask that is the region's trademark.
lines.sale: When the white asparagus arrives, Germany reaches for Silvaner, with its pear, green apple and savoury finish. I would pour it with the asparagus, or with any simply cooked fish.

glass.lead: Pear, green apple and honeydew melon with fresh hay and a savoury, damp earth finish, dry, gentle and unoaked.

ladder.where: Franken, Rheinhessen, Alsace and Alto Adige's Isarco Valley
The sunny, dry Valais in Switzerland, as Johannisberg

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium, gentler than Riesling's, alcohol moderate, body medium; a soft, savoury feel with no new oak.

home.home: Germany, in two regions. Franken, around Würzburg on the river Main, makes it dry and firm on shell limestone and bottles it in the Bocksbeutel. Rheinhessen grows it widely too. It came from Austria, and the first record of it in Germany is from Castell in Franken, in 1659.
home.abroad: Alsace spells it Sylvaner and makes a light, fresh white; one grand cru, Zotzenberg, admits it. Alto Adige grows it high in the Isarco Valley, and the Swiss Valais calls it Johannisberg, a rounder wine with an almond note.

service.temp: 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, 7 to 10 degrees Celsius: cool, not icy, so the gentle scent can show.
service.glass: A white wine glass; nothing wider is needed.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary: pour it cool and fresh.
service.age: Most are for enjoying young, within a few years; the firmest dry wines of Franken keep longer.

with.dish: White asparagus with butter or hollandaise
with.why: gentle acidity and a savoury note suit the spears
a mild wine that does not cover delicate fish
quiet fruit leaves room for the brine
soft, savoury fruit beside salt and smoke

labels.means: The spelling in Alsace, Alto Adige and Switzerland; the same grape.
The flat, round flask of Franken, also allowed in two corners of Baden.
The name for Silvaner in the Swiss canton of Valais; it is not Riesling.
An Alsace grand cru whose rules admit Sylvaner, by exception.

guest.q: What is that odd round bottle?
guest.a: It is the Bocksbeutel, the traditional flask of Franken. The shape is the region's trademark, so when you see it you can expect a dry Franconian wine, very often Silvaner.

guest.q: I have never heard of Silvaner. What is it like?
guest.a: Think of something close to Pinot Blanc but more savoury: dry, with pear and green apple, soft acidity and no oak. It is a wine for food more than for sipping alone.
Rarely. Franken makes it properly dry, and most of what you will meet on a list is dry too.

compare.tell: Müller-Thurgau is lighter and more scented, with elderflower, a faint nutmeg note and softer acidity; Silvaner is firmer, with pear, hay and a savoury finish.
Riesling has piercing acidity, lime and often some sweetness; Silvaner is gentler, dry and savoury, with pear and fresh hay.
Pinot Blanc is rounder, with ripe apple and almond; Silvaner is leaner and more savoury, with green apple, hay and damp earth.

profile.st: Pale straw with green tints · Body medium · Acid medium · Alcohol moderate · Dry; no new oak
profile.fruit: Ripe pear, green apple and quince; white peach and honeydew melon from warmer sites
profile.other: Fresh hay and cut grass, damp earth and celery root; a savoury, gently bitter finish; sweet almond in the Valais
profile.tell: A gentle, dry, savoury white: pear and green apple with fresh hay and damp earth, medium acidity and no loud perfume
profile.regions: Franken (in the Bocksbeutel) and Rheinhessen in Germany; Alsace as Sylvaner, with Zotzenberg; Alto Adige's Isarco Valley; the Valais as Johannisberg
profile.confuse: Riesling has higher acidity and lime; Müller-Thurgau is lighter, with elderflower and nutmeg; Pinot Blanc is rounder, with almond

cards.front: Silvaner: which German region is its home, and in what bottle?
cards.back: Franken, around Würzburg, where it is made dry and bottled in the flat, round Bocksbeutel. Rheinhessen grows it widely too.

cards.front: Silvaner: who are its parents, and when did it reach Germany?
cards.back: A natural cross of Traminer and Österreichisch Weiss, from Austria. It was first planted in Germany, on record, at Castell in Franken, on 6 April 1659.

cards.front: Under what names does Silvaner appear in Alsace and in the Valais?
cards.back: Sylvaner in Alsace, where the grand cru Zotzenberg admits it, and Johannisberg in the Swiss Valais.

questions.q: A guest points to a squat, flat, round flask on the shelf of German wines and asks what is likely to be inside. What do you tell him?
questions.exp: The Bocksbeutel is the flask of Franken, whose signature is dry Silvaner. Mosel Riesling comes in a tall, slim bottle.

questions.q: White asparagus with hollandaise is on the menu, and a guest wants a quiet, dry white that will not fight it. Which grape do you suggest?
questions.exp: Silvaner's gentle acidity and quiet, savoury fruit make it Germany's own match for asparagus. Gewürztraminer, Viognier and Torrontés are loudly perfumed and would cover the dish.

questions.q: A blind white is dry and gentle: pear, green apple and fresh hay, a savoury finish, medium acidity and neither oak nor perfume. Which grape is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: Quiet pear and hay with a savoury finish and only medium acidity point to Silvaner. Riesling would show piercing acidity and lime, and Sauvignon Blanc a loud scent of grapefruit and cut grass.

sources.title: Wines of Germany: highlights of German wine culture, Castell

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it; a thin grape, so it carries its profile. Home is Germany, Franken and Rheinhessen; Alsace, Alto Adige and the Valais stand under abroad.

The Régionale row reads pear, green apple, earthy, herbal: two family words. The entry names fresh hay, mint and cut grass (the German, Alsace and Alto Adige bodies) and damp earth for them. Quince, yellow plum, celery root and green almond are tasting notes of my own, not read in a source this session; a checker may strike them.
The acidity is given as medium, as the Régionale row has it. The German body says mild and the Alsace body vivid; medium, gentler than Riesling's, sits between.
The first record, Castell in Franken on 6 April 1659, stands on the German wine body, one of whose pages gives the purchase as 5 April and the planting as the next day. Castell here is the village.

Johannisberg for the Valais and Zotzenberg admitting Sylvaner are the Codex's own (the Switzerland reading and the Grand Cru bank), so no new source is listed; the Valais growers' page read here adds the sweet almond note.
The ladder keeps Alsace on the cool rung, as the Court's grid read does, and gives the Valais as moderate.
Left out: that Rheinhessen holds the larger area and Franken the larger share, and that Silvaner was once Germany's leading grape, as volatile; any ageing figure, for want of a source.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after seven fixes. A thin grape: its profile stands, in step with the Régionale row. The parentage, the planting at Castell on 6 April 1659, Zotzenberg, Johannisberg and the Bocksbeutel in two corners of Baden were confirmed.
changed: glass.notes, glass.ladder and profile.other: mint is struck. No source read gives it for Silvaner; fresh hay and cut grass stand on tasting notes for Franken wines.
glass.notes: green almond is now bitter almond. The Valais notes read give almond, bitter almond on the finish and a sweet almond nose.
lines.s45: it is a dry white grape is now it makes a dry white; a grape is not dry.
questions[1]: the stem asked for a dry German white and one option, Dornfelder, was a red. The four are now white grapes: Silvaner against Gewürztraminer, Viognier and Torrontés, all loudly perfumed.
questions[0].q: the guest points to the flask on a shelf; nobody points to a flask in a list.

cards[1].back: its first record in Germany is at Castell now reads it was first planted in Germany, on record, at Castell. The German wine body's Castell page, as search quoted it, gives 6 April 1659 as the day twenty five Austrian cuttings were planted at the foot of the Schlossberg; one general reference gives 5 April, the day of the purchase.
compare, the Müller-Thurgau tell, and profile.confuse: more flowery is a family word in disguise; the tell now names elderflower and nutmeg, as that grape's own entry does.
open: Honeydew melon and yellow plum are the German wine body's own words (melons, yellow plums and apples). Quince and celery root are tasting notes with no trade body behind them; root vegetable notes stand in two tasting sources, quince in none read here.
The acidity stays medium, as the Régionale row has it; the German body says mild and other sources say fresh.
